newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Heavy rains seen hitting Colombia coffee crop.
newsitem.headline: Heavy rains seen hitting Colombia coffee crop.

text.p: Torrential rains over the last three weeks in Colombia's principal coffee growing regions are likely to affect the main harvest which begins in October, agronomists said Monday.
The heavy downpours are delaying the flowering period, which should start in January, and in some cases have partially ruined some plantations, regional coffee experts said.

"This recent heavy rain will affect the coffee harvest at the end of the year but the worst effects may be offset if we see sunny periods in February," said Oscar Acevedo, head of the technical division of the Coffee Growers' Committee in central Risaralda province.

Humberto Vanegas, technical assistant at the Coffee Growers' Committee in southwest Valle del Cauca province said the main harvest could be delayed until next January or February but said it was too early to predict how much of the crop could be lost.

In Quindio province, coffee agronomist Csar Corts said the inclement weather was preventing growers from tending to their plantations and could ultimately lead to a rise in production costs as they delayed the start of routine maintenance tasks.
Corts, however, said it was still too early to foresee the precise impact of the unseasonal bad weather.

Heavy rains in late 1995 hit the 1996 early coffee harvest, which is gathered in March and April and accounts for about 40 percent of total production. The harvest was about 500,000 60-kg bags less than initially expected.
The 1996 main harvest, however, was larger than expected and overall production in the 1995-1996 coffee year ended slightly up on forecasts at 12.9 million 60-kg bags.
Last month, the head of the National Coffee Growers' Federation, Jorge Cardenas, forecast output in the 1996-1997 coffee year would be about 12.5 million 60-kg bags.

The rains, which began at the start of the year in a month that is normally hot and dry, have been heaviest in the coffee- growing regions of Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Risaralda, Wquindio, Caldas, Antioquia, Narino and Tolima.

A spokesman at the National Center for the Prevention of Disasters said two people had died, two others had disappeared and about 7,000 families have been displaced by the rains. The weather has sparked widespread mudslides and flooding and caused some smaller rivers to burst their banks.
Dr Humberto Gonzalez, a meteorologist at the national weather center IDEAM, said the causes of the "abnormal"weather pattern were unclear.
He said it may be due to the La Nina effect -- cool currents passing through the Pacific ocean causing higher than normal levels of precipitation.

"These heavy rains are going to continue for at least the next few days but we would expect things to return to normal in February. But because this is such an abnormal situation that we have not seen for at least 10 years, it is very difficult to forecast," Gonzalez said.
He said the weather front would probably move from the west towards central regions of Colombia before breaking up.
